1: Daily Study Bible · The Teacher’s Joy · vv.1–4

Barclay says no New Testament letter shows more plainly that Christian letters followed the pattern everyone used, with a greeting, a prayer for health, the news and the final greetings; he notes that Gaius was the commonest of names, that John cares for body and soul alike, and that a teacher’s greatest joy is to see his pupils walking in the truth.

Says Christians from the earliest times have understood the elder to be the apostle John, and that we do not know whether this Gaius is one of the others in the New Testament, since the name was very common.

Who and what kind of person this Gaius was, is revealed in the course of the Epistle. Because clearly he accumulated good deeds in addition to the faith in Christ which he had received, and although he was not sufficient for preaching the word himself, he rejoiced to sustain those who did preach with his resources.
2: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 1”

Says the wish for prosperity and health was a common phrase of letter writing and is not a guarantee of wealth and perfect health; to walk in truth is to live in a way that matches what one believes, without pretense.

He says, I frequent prayers to the Lord, that you may complete well what you do well. And just as now your soul, that is, the internal intention of your mind prospers, that is, advances in abundant works of alms, and the liberality of a bountiful mind, and the resources of money which you share with the needy, so may you always be able to lead a life full of virtues with the Lord’s help.
3: Daily Study Bible · The Teacher’s Joy · vv.1–4

Barclay says no New Testament letter shows more plainly that Christian letters followed the pattern everyone used, with a greeting, a prayer for health, the news and the final greetings; he notes that Gaius was the commonest of names, that John cares for body and soul alike, and that a teacher’s greatest joy is to see his pupils walking in the truth.

Says the wish for prosperity and health was a common phrase of letter writing and is not a guarantee of wealth and perfect health; to walk in truth is to live in a way that matches what one believes, without pretense.

“you walk in the truth.” He walks in truth who walks in the righteous simplicity of the Gospel. However, to walk does not refer to the motion of limbs, since such steps, passing from one place to another, are common to all animals that have feet; but it signifies an ordered and measured progress according to the keen affection of the mind, which few attain, even among those who are not lacking in understanding.

That is, that I recognize those whom I have begotten to God by preaching or baptizing, observing the truth both of right faith and good operation.
5: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 1”
Daily Study Bible · Christian Hospitality · vv.5–8

Barclay says John’s main purpose is to ask Gaius to receive a group of traveling missionaries and send them on in a Christian way; he describes how poor and ill-famed ancient inns were and how the Christian home became the place of the open door.
You act faithfully, he says, as if he said: Just as you are truly faithful, so you act, showing your faith by your works.
6: Daily Study Bible · Christian Hospitality · vv.5–8

Barclay says John’s main purpose is to ask Gaius to receive a group of traveling missionaries and send them on in a Christian way; he describes how poor and ill-famed ancient inns were and how the Christian home became the place of the open door.
Says hospitality is love in action, that traveling ministers depended on other Christians and took no offerings from the general public, and that those who help them share the work and its reward.
Moreover, this instructs us not to wait for the needy until they come to us, but rather to run to and follow them: like Abraham and Lot.
7: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 1”
Daily Study Bible · The Christian Adventurers · vv.5–8

Barclay says the wandering preachers went out for the sake of the Name and would take nothing from pagans, unlike the begging devotees of other cults, and that those who cannot go themselves can become allies of the truth by supporting those who do.
Says hospitality is love in action, that traveling ministers depended on other Christians and took no offerings from the general public, and that those who help them share the work and its reward.

When it says for the name, it is to be understood as of the Lord Jesus Christ. For the ancients spoke in this manner. And for two reasons, they went out for the name of the Lord, either to preach, evidently coming of their own accord in the name of Him, or because of the faith and confession of the holy name, they were expelled from their homeland by their fellow citizens or relatives.
8: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 1”
Says hospitality is love in action, that traveling ministers depended on other Christians and took no offerings from the general public, and that those who help them share the work and its reward.

But he calls them co-workers of the truth, because he who provides temporal support to those who have spiritual gifts, becomes a co-worker in those spiritual gifts themselves. For since there are few who have received spiritual gifts, and many who are rich in temporal things, by this the rich incorporate themselves into the virtues of the poor, while they share their riches with these holy poor.
9: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 2”
Daily Study Bible · Love’s Appeal · vv.9–14

Barclay sees Diotrephes as the voice of a local congregation that will no longer accept outside authority or traveling preachers; he says we cannot tell what office he held, and that whatever case he had, his fault was a lack of charity.

Diotrephes, it seems, was an arch-heretic of that time, someone proud and insolent, preferring to usurp the preeminence of knowledge by teaching new doctrines, rather than humbly listening to the commands of the ancient holy Church, which John preached.
10: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 2”
Says the problem with Diotrephes was pride; John rebuked him openly and by name, did not excommunicate him, and told Gaius to follow the good example and not the bad.

It should be noted that we should not arouse the tongues of detractors by our fault, lest they perish, but we should equally bear those that are incited by their own malice, so that merit may increase for us; sometimes, however, we should also curb them, lest while they disseminate evil about us, they corrupt the hearts of the innocent who could have heard good things.
11: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 2”
Daily Study Bible · Love’s Appeal · vv.9–14

Barclay thinks Demetrius was probably the leader of the traveling preachers and the bearer of the letter, which is why John gives him a testimonial; he mentions, without settling on them, guesses that he was the silversmith of Ephesus or Demas.
Says the problem with Diotrephes was pride; John rebuked him openly and by name, did not excommunicate him, and told Gaius to follow the good example and not the bad.

Since there is no unity of light with darkness, nor any unity between Christ and Belial (2 Cor. 6:14), it is not appropriate for one who has been illuminated by the knowledge of Christ to mix with darkness through the imitation of the wicked, or through their lustful and shameless works.
12: Daily Study Bible · Love’s Appeal · vv.9–14

Barclay thinks Demetrius was probably the leader of the traveling preachers and the bearer of the letter, which is why John gives him a testimonial; he mentions, without settling on them, guesses that he was the silversmith of Ephesus or Demas.
Says John recommends Demetrius, who perhaps carried the letter, as worthy of hospitality, a man so faithful that the truth itself is a witness for him.
That is, he himself welcomed the weak and supported the needy for the sake of the truth. Therefore, Gaius should also imitate him, so that he too may be worthy of the praise of all.
13: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 2”
Daily Study Bible · Love’s Appeal · vv.9–14
Barclay says John ends in love: he will soon come and talk, since his presence can do what no letter can, and meanwhile he sends his greetings and a blessing of peace to a troubled church.
Says we can sympathize with John’s wish to speak face to face, and that a letter about conflict fittingly ends with peace and with a reminder that Christians far apart are still friends.
The reason for the briefness of the letter, both in this and in the following one, is that John hoped to come to them and to add in person and by his presence what was lacking.
14: “Friends and Foes in the Church, Part 2”
Daily Study Bible · Love’s Appeal · vv.9–14
Barclay says John ends in love: he will soon come and talk, since his presence can do what no letter can, and meanwhile he sends his greetings and a blessing of peace to a troubled church.
He sends greetings of peace and health to friends, showing by this that Diotrephes and other enemies of the truth are foreign to your peace and salvation.
